errata.notes:
According to ABNF, 0<pchar> is interpreted as
zero repeatation of the prose-val: pchar.

However pchar is an non-terminal.
So I think the production should be follows:
  path-empty = 0pchar

However this production means a empty string.
So
  path-empty = ""
is more clear.

Appendix A. has also the same production.

errata.orig: Advice for designers of new URI schemes can be found in [RFC2718].
errata.correct: Advice for designers of new URI schemes can be found in [RFC4395].
errata.notes:
The document [RFC2718] is for designers of designers of new URL schemes only.  It has been obsoleted by [RFC4395] that covers all URI schemes.

[RFC4395]
T. Hansen, T. Hardie, T. and L. Masinter,
"Guidelines and Registration Procedures for New URI Schemes",
RFC 4395, February 2006.
This is a copy of Erratum #1933, reported against RFC 2396.

In 5.2.3. the "If the base URI has a defined authority component" condition requires knowing the authority component, so passing just the path component is misleading.

During discussion of this issue, Roy Fielding noted: "No, this is not an error in the algorithm.  The algorithm is just saying that you need to merge the two paths.  The two paths are not parameters to a function, nor is the merge procedure limited to those two parameters." Saving this report as "Hold For Document Update" so that future implementers do not experience the same confusion.

errata.orig:
5.4.2.  Abnormal Examples

   Although the following abnormal examples are unlikely to occur in
   normal practice, all URI parsers should be capable of resolving them
   consistently.  Each example uses the same base as that above.

   Parsers must be careful in handling cases where there are more ".."
   segments in a relative-path reference than there are hierarchical
   levels in the base URI's path.  Note that the ".." syntax cannot be
   used to change the authority component of a URI.

      "../../../g"    =  "http://a/g"
      "../../../../g" =  "http://a/g"
errata.correct:
5.4.2.  Abnormal Examples

   Although the following abnormal examples are unlikely to occur in
   normal practice, all URI parsers should be capable of resolving them
   consistently.  Each example uses the same base as that above.

   Parsers must be careful in handling cases where there are more ".."
   segments in a relative-path reference than there are hierarchical
   levels in the base URI's path.  Note that the ".." syntax cannot be
   used to change the authority component of a URI.

      "../../../g"    =  "http://a/../g"
      "../../../../g" =  "http://a/../../g"
errata.notes:
The example which was taken from RFC 1808 had proper resolved URL ( 5.2 ).

As the base URL has two levels ( http://a/b/c/ ) and if the relative url's have two ".." segments then from the resolved URI both the hierarchical levels can be removed to form the resolved URL, as below:

../../g    = http://a/g

and if there are more ".." segments than hierarchical level in base URI's path... then the number of ".." segments that doesn't have corresponding segments in base URI should be left as is in the resolved URI,  like below

"../../../g" = "http://a/../g"

errata.orig:
Characters that are allowed in a URI but do not have a reserved purpose are called unreserved.  These include uppercase and lowercase letters, decimal digits, hyphen, period, underscore, and tilde.

      unreserved  = ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "." / "_" / "~"
errata.correct:
Characters that are allowed in a URI but do not have a reserved purpose are called unreserved.  These include uppercase and lowercase letters, decimal digits, hyphen, period, underscore, tilde, and backslash

      unreserved  = ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "." / "_" / "~" | "\"
errata.notes:
The ASCII backslash character seems to have been left out of the set of unreserved characters.

The backslash character doesn't have any reserved use (per its not appearing in the reserved EBNF production and not being used anywhere else in URI-reference syntax).

Therefore, backslash appears to be an unreserved character, per section 2.3's text "Characters that are allowed in a URI but do not have a reserved purpose are called unreserved."

However, backslash is not mentioned explicitly in section 2.3, neither in the the text referring to several individual characters by name nor in the grammar production specifying those characters.

So the current text is _unclear_ regarding whether backslashes are allowed in URLs (e.g., within a path segment (between segment-separating (forward) slashes)).

SO ... that should be clarified. Either backslash should be added to the text (prose and EBNF) of section 2.3, or there should be a clear mention that backslash is not allowed.

Although using backslashes in a URI reference might be unusual, it's not clear that there's any reason to exclude them. (If a server/URI authority wants to use backslashes in (non-reserved parts of) URLs, is there any reason that it should be blocked from doing so?)

Therefore, it seems that the choice should be to specify backslashes as allowed.
